title: Ezra 2:36–58
context: The list turns from the lay houses to the temple ministers: four priestly families, a small body of Levites, the singers of Asaph, the gatekeepers, the temple servants, and the children of Solomon’s servants. The four priestly houses agree in name and number with Nehemiah 7:39–42. The Levites are seventy-four in both lists, though this verse has Hodaviah and Nehemiah 7:43 has Hodevah. The singers and gatekeepers differ by small amounts, one hundred twenty-eight and one hundred thirty-nine here, one hundred forty-eight and one hundred thirty-eight in Nehemiah 7:44–45. The long run of temple-servant names has many small spelling differences, and a few names sit in a different order; the combined total of temple servants and Solomon’s servants is three hundred ninety-two in both books. Those differences should be named, not harmonized, and they do not make a theological contrast. Both traditions read the unit as a record of the people set apart for the house, a much smaller company than the lay enrollment, and they leave the two lists side by side.

verses.text: The priests: the children of Jedaiah, of the house of Jeshua, nine hundred seventy-three.
verses.arminianNotes:
The priests begin with the children of Jedaiah, of the house of Jeshua, nine hundred seventy-three, the same count as Nehemiah 7:39. Jeshua has already appeared as a leader in 2:2; here a priestly house is named after his house, and the notes do not confuse every later Jeshua with that one man.

Arminian readers take nine hundred seventy-three as a real priestly enrollment, the first of four houses.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the agreement with Nehemiah 7:39 and read the line as the first priestly count, not as a symbol of later priesthood.

Both traditions invent no contrast over a matching figure and keep Jeshua’s house as the text names it.

verses.text: The children of Immer, one thousand fifty-two.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Immer number one thousand fifty-two, the same count as Nehemiah 7:40. Immer is a known priestly house from earlier lists, and the two return lists agree on the figure.

Arminian readers take the number as the enrollment of this priestly family in the return.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also record the matching total and leave the line in the register of the list, a second priestly house beside Jedaiah.

Both traditions invent no contrast over a count that agrees, and they do not allegorize the name.

verses.text: The children of Pashhur, one thousand two hundred forty-seven.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Pashhur number one thousand two hundred forty-seven, the same count as Nehemiah 7:41, and the largest of the four priestly houses in this unit.

Arminian readers take one thousand two hundred forty-seven as a historical enrollment, not as a cue for a moral lesson in the size of the house.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the agreement with Nehemiah 7:41 and keep the figure as a count of priests who came up.

Both traditions refuse to turn the largest priestly total into a symbol, and they invent no contrast over a matching number.

verses.text: The children of Harim, one thousand seventeen.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Harim number one thousand seventeen, the same count as Nehemiah 7:42. This priestly Harim is not the lay Harim of 2:32, whose count was three hundred twenty.

Arminian readers keep the two Harim lines distinct and take one thousand seventeen as the priestly enrollment given here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also distinguish this house from the earlier lay family of the same name, and they note the agreement with Nehemiah 7:42.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the shared priestly figure, and they do not merge the two Harim entries.

verses.text: The Levites: the children of Jeshua and Kadmiel, of the children of Hodaviah, seventy-four.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Levites are the children of Jeshua and Kadmiel, of the children of Hodaviah, seventy-four, a very small company beside the priests. Nehemiah 7:43 has the same total, with the name Hodevah rather than Hodaviah. The difference is in the spelling, not in the count.

Arminian readers take seventy-four as the real Levitical return in this list, and they keep WEB’s Hodaviah here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also report the agreed total and the changed form Hodevah in Nehemiah 7:43, without forcing one spelling.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the name, and they do not hide how few Levites are listed.

verses.text: The singers: the children of Asaph, one hundred twenty-eight.
verses.arminianNotes:
The singers are the children of Asaph, one hundred twenty-eight. Nehemiah 7:44 has one hundred forty-eight for the same Asaph company. The two figures should be named and left unharmonized.

Arminian readers keep this verse’s one hundred twenty-eight and refuse to correct it from the other list.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also set the two singer totals side by side and treat the difference as a fact of the lists, not as a doctrinal issue.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the counts and do not turn Asaph’s name into a type.

verses.text: The children of the gatekeepers: the children of Shallum, the children of Ater, the children of Talmon, the children of Akkub, the children of Hatita, the children of Shobai, in all one hundred thirty-nine.
verses.arminianNotes:
The gatekeepers are the children of Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita, and Shobai, in all one hundred thirty-nine. Nehemiah 7:45 names the same six houses and gives one hundred thirty-eight. The names agree; the totals differ by one and should be left as they stand.

Arminian readers take one hundred thirty-nine as this book’s count of the gatekeepers, and they do not replace it with the other figure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also report both totals and the shared names, and they refuse to treat a difference of one as a theological problem.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the counts and keep the six houses as the lists give them.

verses.text: The temple servants: the children of Ziha, the children of Hasupha, the children of Tabbaoth,
verses.arminianNotes:
The temple servants begin with the children of Ziha, Hasupha, and Tabbaoth, the first names in a long run that continues through 2:54. Nehemiah 7:46 opens with the same three names. Individual counts are not given for these houses; the combined total comes later, in 2:58.

Arminian readers take the names as a real enrollment of temple servants, listed by houses, not as a coded roster.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start this servant list with the same opening names as Nehemiah 7, and they wait for the total in 2:58.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the names and do not assign a hidden meaning to the first three houses.

verses.text: the children of Keros, the children of Siaha, the children of Padon,
verses.arminianNotes:
The list continues with the children of Keros, Siaha, and Padon. Nehemiah 7:47 has Keros, Sia, and Padon, a shorter form of the middle name. No separate figures are given.

Arminian readers keep WEB’s Siaha here and record the parallel spelling without rewriting the verse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also set Siaha and Sia side by side and leave the names as a part of the same servant list, still waiting for the combined total.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the spelling and do not invent counts the verse does not supply.

verses.text: the children of Lebanah, the children of Hagabah, the children of Akkub,
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Lebanah, Hagabah, and Akkub follow. Nehemiah 7:48 has Lebana, Hagaba, and then Salmai, a different third name in that slot, while an Akkub has already appeared among the gatekeepers in 2:42. The notes report the difference and do not force the two sequences into one.

Arminian readers keep Lebanah, Hagabah, and Akkub as this verse names them, without substituting the Nehemiah third name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the spelling differences and the changed third name unharmonized, and they do not identify this Akkub with the gatekeeper house as if the list had said so.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the names and refuse to merge the rosters.

verses.text: the children of Hagab, the children of Shamlai, the children of Hanan,
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Hagab, Shamlai, and Hanan are named next. Nehemiah 7 places related names in a slightly different order and has Salmai in the preceding line, as already noted. The houses are listed, not numbered, and the notes do not invent a reason for every shift of order.

Arminian readers take the three names as this verse’s contribution to the servant list, and they refuse to rearrange them from the other book.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep Hagab, Shamlai, and Hanan here, and they treat the small differences of order and spelling in Nehemiah 7 as facts to be named, not corrected.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the roster and wait for the total in 2:58.

verses.text: the children of Giddel, the children of Gahar, the children of Reaiah,
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Giddel, Gahar, and Reaiah continue the same servant list. Related names appear in Nehemiah 7:49–50, again without separate counts. The line is part of the catalog, not a place to build a doctrine of service.

Arminian readers take the three houses as a further real enrollment of temple servants in the return.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read the names as a continuation of the list already begun, to be compared with Nehemiah 7 and not rewritten from it.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the spellings and do not assign a symbolic sense to the houses.

verses.text: the children of Rezin, the children of Nekoda, the children of Gazzam,
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Rezin, Nekoda, and Gazzam follow. A Nekoda will appear again among those who cannot show their descent, in 2:60; the notes do not assume that these are the same house. Nehemiah 7 also lists Rezin, Nekoda, and Gazzam among the temple servants, in a slightly different order.

Arminian readers keep this Nekoda in the servant list where the verse places it, and they do not prejudge the later name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also report the parallel names in Nehemiah 7 and leave the later Nekoda of 2:60 as a separate question until that verse.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the names and refuse to merge two lines that the list itself keeps apart.

verses.text: the children of Uzza, the children of Paseah, the children of Besai,
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Uzza, Paseah, and Besai continue the catalog. The same three names appear among the temple servants in Nehemiah 7:51–52, still without individual figures.

Arminian readers take the houses as a further part of the historical roster, not as names chosen for a hidden meaning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also set the three names beside the Nehemiah parallel and leave them unnumbered until the combined total.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the wording and do not press the names into a type.

verses.text: the children of Asnah, the children of Meunim, the children of Nephisim,
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Asnah, Meunim, and Nephisim are named next. Nehemiah 7:52 has Meunim and Nephushesim, a longer form of the third name, and Asnah is not named in the same way there. The differences should be reported and left as they stand.

Arminian readers keep Asnah, Meunim, and Nephisim as this verse records them, without dropping or reshaping a name to match the other list.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name the changed form Nephushesim and the uneven overlap with Nehemiah 7, and they refuse to force a single reconstructed roster.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the spellings and do not invent a count for these houses.

verses.text: the children of Bakbuk, the children of Hakupha, the children of Harhur,
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Bakbuk, Hakupha, and Harhur follow, and the same three names stand in Nehemiah 7:53. Here the two lists agree in this short run, still without separate numbers.

Arminian readers take the three houses as a real part of the servant enrollment, matching the parallel in these names.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the agreement in this line of names and keep the verse in the ordinary register of the list.

Both traditions invent no contrast where the rosters match, and they still wait for the combined total.

verses.text: the children of Bazluth, the children of Mehida, the children of Harsha,
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Bazluth, Mehida, and Harsha are named next. Nehemiah 7:54 has Bazlith, Mehida, and Harsha, a small difference in the first name and the same two that follow.

Arminian readers keep WEB’s Bazluth here and record Bazlith as the parallel form, without substituting it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave Bazluth and Bazlith unharmonized and treat Mehida and Harsha as shared names in the same list of servants.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the spelling and do not assign figures the verse does not give.

verses.text: the children of Barkos, the children of Sisera, the children of Temah,
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Barkos, Sisera, and Temah continue the list, and the same three names appear in Nehemiah 7:55. The run of close agreement in these last servant houses is part of the record, not a lesson in itself.

Arminian readers take the three names as a further historical enrollment of temple servants.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the matching names in Nehemiah 7:55 and leave the line unnumbered until 2:58.

Both traditions invent no contrast over an agreeing run of names, and they refuse to allegorize them.

verses.text: the children of Neziah, the children of Hatipha.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Neziah and Hatipha close the temple-servant names, as in Nehemiah 7:56. Still no separate counts are given; the next verses turn to Solomon’s servants before the combined total.

Arminian readers take Neziah and Hatipha as the last houses in this stretch of the servant list, a real close of the catalog of names.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the agreement with Nehemiah 7:56 and keep the two names as the end of the temple-servant roster in both books.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the closing names and wait for the figure in 2:58.

verses.text: The children of Solomon’s servants: the children of Sotai, the children of Hassophereth, the children of Peruda,
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Solomon’s servants begin with Sotai, Hassophereth, and Peruda. Nehemiah 7:57 has Sotai, Sophereth, and Perida, shorter or slightly altered forms of the second and third names. The phrase “Solomon’s servants” is the heading this list uses; the notes do not invent a full history of the group beyond what is written.

Arminian readers keep Hassophereth and Peruda as WEB gives them, and they record the parallel spellings without rewriting the verse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also set the two forms side by side and treat the heading as a historical class within the return, not as a symbol of later servitude.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the names and do not fill in a story the verse does not tell.

verses.text: the children of Jaalah, the children of Darkon, the children of Giddel,
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Jaalah, Darkon, and Giddel follow among Solomon’s servants. Nehemiah 7:58 has Jaala, Darkon, and Giddel, a shorter form of the first name. A Giddel has already appeared among the temple servants in 2:47; the list uses the name again here without saying the houses are one.

Arminian readers keep Jaalah as this verse’s form and refuse to identify the two Giddel lines as if the text had joined them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also report Jaala in Nehemiah 7:58 and leave the repeated Giddel name unmerged, a question the lists themselves do not answer.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the spelling and do not invent a single house from two entries.

verses.text: the children of Shephatiah, the children of Hattil, the children of Pochereth Hazzebaim, the children of Ami.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Shephatiah, Hattil, Pochereth Hazzebaim, and Ami close the names of Solomon’s servants. Nehemiah 7:59 has Shephatiah, Hattil, Pochereth Hazzebaim, and Amon, the same first three and a different last name, Ami here and Amon there. A Shephatiah has already appeared as a lay house in 2:4.

Arminian readers keep Ami as the name written here, and they do not substitute Amon or merge this Shephatiah with the earlier lay family.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave Ami and Amon unharmonized and treat the rest of the line as shared wording, including the compound name Pochereth Hazzebaim.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the last name and refuse to collapse two Shephatiah entries into one.

verses.text: All the temple servants, and the children of Solomon’s servants, were three hundred ninety-two.
verses.arminianNotes:
“All the temple servants, and the children of Solomon’s servants, were three hundred ninety-two.” The combined total agrees with Nehemiah 7:60. No breakdown between the two groups is given in either list. The company is small beside the lay houses and the priests, and the number is not a symbol.

Arminian readers take three hundred ninety-two as the real combined enrollment, a figure in which the two books meet after many small differences of name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the agreed total and leave the unsplit figure as the text gives it, without inventing subtotals for the two classes.

Both traditions close the minister list on that shared count, without a contrast over the names that have differed along the way.
